assessments.title: Frontend Architecture & React Patterns
assessments.description: Test your knowledge of state management, component lifecycles, and performance optimization in React 18+.

questions.question: When would using `useCallback` be actively detrimental to performance in React?
options: When passed to an HTML button element with an inline handler
When passed to a memoized child component (React.memo)
When wrapping every function without passing to optimized children, adding unnecessary closure overhead
When used inside a Custom Hook
questions.explanation: useCallback has non-zero memory and compute overhead. If the child component is not wrapped in React.memo or the function isn't a dependency of an effect, useCallback costs more than re-creating a lightweight function.

questions.question: How does React 18 Concurrent Mode handle high-priority UI updates vs background renders?
options: Via `useTransition` and `useDeferredValue` which yield to the main thread during heavy rendering
By pausing JavaScript event loops completely
By server-side rendering all components immediately
questions.explanation: Concurrent React introduces interruptible rendering with useTransition and useDeferredValue, prioritizing urgent user inputs over non-urgent UI transitions.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of Zustand over traditional Redux without toolkit?
options: Zustand eliminates boilerplate, avoids Context provider wrappers, and allows transient updates without re-renders
Zustand does not support async actions
questions.explanation: Zustand uses a hook-based pub/sub model with zero provider boilerplate, supports fine-grained selector subscriptions, and handles async cleanly.

questions.question: What does TypeScript `ReturnType<T>` utility type do?
options: Returns the number of arguments in function T
Constructs a type consisting of the return type of function T
Executes function T at compile time
questions.explanation: ReturnType<T> extracts the returned type of a function signature using type inference with `infer`.

questions.question: Why should keys in React lists never be assigned as `Math.random()` or array index when items reorder?
options: Because React throws a syntax error
Because index keys cause DOM reconciliation bugs and random keys cause total DOM unmounting/remounting on every render
Because Tailwind CSS cannot style elements with random keys
Because keys are sent to the backend server
questions.explanation: React relies on stable keys for diffing. Random keys destroy component state on each render, and indices cause state to be bound to the wrong items during insertions/deletions.

questions.question: Which HTTP method is defined as NOT idempotent?
questions.explanation: POST is not idempotent because repeating the identical request typically creates duplicate resources, whereas PUT and DELETE have idempotent side-effects.

questions.question: What is the most appropriate HTTP status code when a client requests a resource that exists but they lack permissions?
questions.explanation: 401 means unauthenticated (who are you?), while 403 Forbidden means authenticated but insufficient authorization (you are not allowed).

questions.question: What header is used in CORS preflight checks to declare allowed custom headers?
questions.explanation: Access-Control-Allow-Headers specifies which HTTP headers can be used during the actual request.

questions.question: What is the recommended payload format for partial updates in RESTful services?
options: HTTP PATCH with JSON Merge Patch or JSON Patch
questions.explanation: HTTP PATCH is designed specifically for applying partial modifications to a resource.

questions.title: JavaScript Event Loop & Microtasks
questions.prompt: In JavaScript's concurrency model, what is the execution priority between `Promise.resolve().then(...)` (Microtask queue) and `setTimeout(..., 0)` (Macrotask queue) after the current synchronous call stack empties?
questions.explanation: Microtasks (resolved Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) are always completely drained before the event loop picks the next macrotask (such as setTimeout/setInterval).

options.text: The Promise callback executes before the setTimeout callback.
options.explanation: Microtask queue executes immediately after synchronous code.

options.text: The setTimeout callback executes first because it has a 0ms timer.
options.explanation: Timers go to the macrotask queue, which yields to microtasks.

options.text: They run simultaneously on parallel CPU threads.
options.explanation: JavaScript runtime execution is single-threaded on the main thread.

options.text: The execution order is completely non-deterministic.
options.explanation: The ECMAScript specification defines strict queue order.

questions.title: React useEffect Dependency Invalidation
questions.prompt: Why does passing an inline object (e.g. `{ id: userId }`) inside a React `useEffect` dependency array frequently cause infinite re-render loops if state updates occur inside the effect?
questions.explanation: In JavaScript, objects are compared by referential identity (Object.is), not deep value equality. On every component render, a new object reference in memory is created, causing React to treat the dependency as changed every render.

options.text: Inline object literals create a new memory reference on every render, failing referential equality check (Object.is).
options.explanation: React uses Object.is referential comparison for dependency checking.

options.text: React useEffect only supports primitive numbers in dependency arrays.
options.explanation: Objects are allowed, but will trigger on every reference change.

options.text: React freezes all objects declared inside JSX.
options.explanation: React does not freeze inline object references.

options.text: Objects in dependencies automatically mutate state synchronously.
options.explanation: Dependencies do not mutate state; they only control trigger conditions.

questions.title: SQL Indexing B-Tree vs Hash
questions.prompt: Which query pattern benefits from a standard B-Tree database index but CANNOT utilize a Hash index?
questions.explanation: Hash indexes only support direct equality operators (=, <=>) because hash functions scatter keys non-linearly. B-Tree indexes keep keys sorted, making range scans (BETWEEN, >, <) and prefix searches extremely efficient.

options.text: Range queries such as `WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-06-30'`
options.explanation: Hash indexes cannot preserve ordering for range comparisons.

options.text: Exact match lookups such as `WHERE user_id = 452`
options.explanation: Hash indexes are optimal for exact equality lookups.

options.text: Boolean lookups such as `WHERE is_active = true`
options.explanation: Hash indexes can evaluate equality matches.

options.text: Primary key joins with identical IDs
options.explanation: Primary key equality joins can use hash indexes.

questions.title: ACID Isolation Levels & Phantom Reads
questions.prompt: In relational database management systems (RDBMS), which SQL transaction isolation level guarantees protection against 'Phantom Reads' (where re-running a range query finds new rows inserted by another concurrent transaction)?
questions.explanation: SERIALIZABLE is the highest isolation level and prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads (typically using range locks or multiversion concurrency control serializability checks).

options.text: SERIALIZABLE
options.explanation: Serializable isolation enforces predicate locks preventing new phantom row insertions.

options.text: READ COMMITTED
options.explanation: Read Committed allows both non-repeatable reads and phantom reads.

options.text: REPEATABLE READ (Standard ANSI)
options.explanation: In standard ANSI SQL, Repeatable Read protects row modifications but permits phantom row inserts.

options.text: READ UNCOMMITTED
options.explanation: Read Uncommitted is vulnerable to dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantoms.

questions.title: HTTP/2 Multiplexing vs HTTP/1.1 Head-of-Line Blocking
questions.prompt: How does HTTP/2 solve the application-layer Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking problem present in HTTP/1.1?
questions.explanation: HTTP/2 introduces a binary framing layer that breaks request and response messages down into independent, interleaved frames over a single shared TCP connection.

options.text: By breaking HTTP messages into binary frames that can be multiplexed concurrently over a single TCP connection.
options.explanation: Binary framing allows interleaved streams without waiting for preceding responses.

options.text: By opening 50 separate TCP socket connections per domain name simultaneously.
options.explanation: Opening multiple connections was the HTTP/1.1 workaround, not HTTP/2 multiplexing.

options.text: By replacing TCP entirely with UDP datagram packets.
options.explanation: Replacing TCP with UDP (QUIC) is the feature of HTTP/3, not HTTP/2.

options.text: By compressing request bodies with Gzip automatically.
options.explanation: HPACK handles header compression, but multiplexing solves HoL blocking.

questions.title: Docker Layer Caching Optimization
questions.prompt: In a Node.js Dockerfile, why is it recommended to copy `package.json` and run `npm install` BEFORE copying the entire project source directory (`COPY . .`)?
questions.explanation: Docker caches each build step layer. If source code changes but package.json remains untouched, Docker can reuse the cached `npm install` layer, accelerating build times from minutes to seconds.

options.text: To maximize Docker layer caching so dependencies are not reinstalled when only application source code changes.
options.explanation: Docker reuses cached layers up until the first step where file hashes change.

options.text: Because npm install cannot access files in the root folder.
options.explanation: npm install only needs package.json/package-lock.json.

options.text: To prevent TypeScript files from being compiled into the container.
options.explanation: Layer ordering does not determine file compilation.

options.text: Because Docker containers cannot write to disk after COPY commands.
options.explanation: Containers remain writable during all RUN steps in multi-stage builds.

questions.title: Git Rebase vs Git Merge
questions.prompt: What is the primary difference in Git commit history when integrating a feature branch using `git rebase main` compared to `git merge main`?
questions.explanation: `git rebase` replays your feature commits on top of the tip of the target branch, creating a linear, chronological commit history without generating an extra merge commit.

options.text: Rebase rewrites commit history to create a clean, linear sequence, whereas merge preserves exact commit timestamps and creates a dedicated merge commit.
options.explanation: Rebasing creates new commit hashes replayed on top of the upstream branch.

options.text: Rebase deletes all past commit messages permanently.
options.explanation: Rebase preserves commit messages unless interactive squash is requested.

options.text: Merge is only possible between remote repositories on GitHub.
options.explanation: Merge is a core local Git operation.

options.text: Rebase automatically resolves all merge conflicts without developer input.
options.explanation: Conflicts must still be resolved during each replayed commit.

questions.title: Python GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) Concurrency
questions.prompt: How does CPython's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) affect multi-threaded CPU-bound programs in Python?
questions.explanation: The GIL ensures that only one native OS thread executes Python bytecode at any single instant within a single interpreter process. For CPU-bound tasks, multi-threading cannot leverage multiple CPU cores; the `multiprocessing` module is required instead.

options.text: It restricts bytecode execution to a single CPU core at any given time, preventing CPU-bound threads from achieving true multi-core parallelism.
options.explanation: CPython GIL serializes bytecode execution across threads in a process.

options.text: It prevents Python from making asynchronous HTTP network calls.
options.explanation: I/O bound operations release the GIL while waiting.

options.text: It forces all Python variables to become immutable.
options.explanation: GIL manages memory safety, not object mutability.

options.text: It disables garbage collection during loop executions.
options.explanation: Reference counting and cyclical GC operate alongside the GIL.

questions.title: Java Memory Model: Heap vs Stack
questions.prompt: In the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), where are object instances allocated versus local primitive variable declarations?
questions.explanation: In the JVM, all object instances reside on the shared Garbage Collected Heap, while local primitive variables and method call execution frames reside on the per-thread Call Stack.

options.text: Object instances are allocated on the Heap; local primitive variables are stored on the thread's Stack.
options.explanation: The Heap stores reference types; thread execution stacks store local primitives.

options.text: All variables and objects are stored exclusively on the Stack.
options.explanation: Stack memory cannot accommodate dynamic lifetime objects.

options.text: Primitive variables reside on the Heap, while classes reside in CPU cache.
options.explanation: Local primitives are allocated within stack frames.

options.text: The JVM does not separate Heap and Stack memory.
options.explanation: The JVM specification explicitly separates Heap and Stack regions.

questions.title: REST Idempotency
questions.prompt: Which of the following HTTP methods is defined by the HTTP/1.1 specification as strictly IDEMPOTENT (making multiple identical requests produces the exact same server state as a single request)?
questions.explanation: PUT and DELETE are idempotent because executing `PUT /users/1` or `DELETE /users/1` multiple times results in the same end state on the server. POST is not idempotent as repeated calls create multiple resources.

options.text: PUT and DELETE
options.explanation: Repeating PUT or DELETE results in the same resource state.

options.text: POST and PATCH
options.explanation: POST creates new records on repeat; PATCH can apply relative increments.

options.text: Only POST
options.explanation: POST is explicitly non-idempotent.

options.text: HTTP specification does not define idempotency for any method.
options.explanation: RFC 7231 specifically defines idempotent methods.

questions.title: TypeScript Discriminated Unions
questions.prompt: What is a 'Discriminated Union' (tagged union) in TypeScript and how does it assist type narrowing?
questions.explanation: A discriminated union is a union of object types where each type shares a common literal property (the discriminant, such as `type: 'success' | 'error'`). TypeScript's control flow analysis uses this tag to narrow down specific object shapes in switch or if statements.

options.text: A union of types sharing a common literal discriminator field, enabling TypeScript to narrow types accurately in conditional branches.
options.explanation: The shared literal property acts as a type guard for compiler narrowing.

options.text: A method of converting JavaScript numbers to binary strings.
options.explanation: This describes radix formatting, not union types.

options.text: A mechanism that hides private class variables at runtime.
options.explanation: Discriminated unions are compile-time structural typing constructs.

options.text: A tool to merge CSS stylesheets into TypeScript definitions.
options.explanation: Unions describe data types, not styling modules.

questions.title: Web Accessibility (a11y) ARIA Labels
questions.prompt: When designing an accessible icon-only button (e.g. `<button><svg>...</svg></button>`), what is the best practice to ensure screen reader assistive technologies can convey the button's purpose?
questions.explanation: Icon buttons lack readable text nodes. Providing an `aria-label="Close dialog"` attribute gives screen readers descriptive text to announce to visually impaired users.

options.text: Add an `aria-label` attribute describing the specific action (e.g. `aria-label="Close modal"`).
options.explanation: aria-label provides accessible naming for interactive elements without visible text.

options.text: Add an inline CSS hover tooltip with `title`.
options.explanation: title attributes are not reliably announced and fail touch screen accessibility.

options.text: Change the button element to a generic `<div>` with `onclick`.
options.explanation: Non-semantic divs lose keyboard focus and ARIA button roles.

options.text: Apply CSS `display: none` to the icon.
options.explanation: Hiding the icon removes it from visual rendering altogether.

questions.title: Database Normalization (3NF)
questions.prompt: A database table is considered to be in Third Normal Form (3NF) if it is already in 2NF and satisfies which key condition?
questions.explanation: Third Normal Form requires that every non-prime attribute is non-transitively dependent on every candidate key (no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute).

options.text: It contains no transitive functional dependencies (no non-key attribute determines another non-key attribute).
options.explanation: 3NF eliminates transitive dependencies between non-primary attributes.

options.text: Every column contains a JSON formatted document.
options.explanation: JSON columns often violate 1NF atomicity.

options.text: It possesses at least 3 foreign key constraints.
options.explanation: Foreign key count does not determine normalization level.

options.text: All columns are declared with NOT NULL constraints.
options.explanation: Nullable columns are permitted in 3NF.

questions.title: Linux File Permissions & Octal Masks
questions.prompt: In a Linux terminal, what permissions does executing `chmod 754 script.sh` grant to the User (Owner), Group, and Others respectively?
questions.explanation: 7 = Read(4)+Write(2)+Execute(1) (rwx for owner). 5 = Read(4)+Execute(1) (r-x for group). 4 = Read(4) (r-- for others).

options.text: User: Read/Write/Execute (rwx), Group: Read/Execute (r-x), Others: Read-only (r--)
User: Read-only, Group: Write-only, Others: Execute-only
options.explanation: Octal permissions sum binary bit flags.

options.text: User: Read/Write, Group: Read/Write, Others: Read/Write
options.explanation: Full read/write is 666.

options.text: All users receive root administrator execution access
options.explanation: Permissions are scoped specifically to owner/group/other masks.

questions.title: Software Testing Pyramid
questions.prompt: According to the industry-standard Testing Pyramid principle, how should a test suite be distributed for optimal speed, cost, and reliability?
questions.explanation: The pyramid advocates for a large foundation of fast, inexpensive Unit Tests, a moderate middle layer of Integration/API tests, and a lean top tier of End-to-End (E2E) UI tests.

options.text: A broad base of fast Unit tests, a moderate layer of Integration tests, and a minimal set of End-to-End UI tests.
options.explanation: Unit tests are fast and deterministic, while E2E tests are slower and prone to flakiness.

options.text: 100% End-to-End UI tests and zero unit tests.
options.explanation: An inverted pyramid leads to brittle, slow CI pipelines.

options.text: Only manual exploratory testing performed right before deployment.
options.explanation: Automated regression suites are essential for continuous delivery.

options.text: Equal 33% distribution across unit, integration, and load tests.
options.explanation: Unit tests should always outnumber higher-level tests.

questions.title: Scenario: Node.js Memory Leak in Event Listeners
questions.explanation: Every incoming HTTP request adds a new listener function closure referencing `res` to the global `notificationHub`. When clients disconnect or abort, the listener is never removed, preventing the garbage collector from reclaiming response objects. The fix is to listen for `req.on('close', () => notificationHub.removeListener('broadcast', onNewData))`.

options.text: The event listener references the `res` closure and is never removed when the client disconnects. Fix: Bind `req.on('close', ...)` to remove the listener.
options.explanation: Unregistered event listeners retain closures in heap memory indefinitely.

options.text: Express does not support JSON.stringify inside route handlers.
options.explanation: JSON stringification is standard in streams.

options.text: Node.js EventEmitters cannot be instantiated as constants.
options.explanation: Const variables do not cause memory leaks.

options.text: The route path must end in '.json' to avoid memory leaks.
options.explanation: URL naming has no bearing on V8 heap memory.

questions.title: Scenario: Database N+1 Query Anti-Pattern
questions.prompt:
An API endpoint fetching 50 blog posts takes 4.2 seconds to load. Server logs show 51 separate SQL queries generated for a single HTTP request:
1. `SELECT * FROM posts LIMIT 50;`
2. `SELECT * FROM authors WHERE id = 1;`
3. `SELECT * FROM authors WHERE id = 2;`
... (repeated 50 times in a loop)

What database optimization technique eliminates this performance bottleneck?
questions.explanation: This is the classic N+1 query problem. Instead of executing an isolated query inside a loop for each parent record, you should execute an eager JOIN (`SELECT * FROM posts JOIN authors ON posts.author_id = authors.id`) or a single batch lookup (`SELECT * FROM authors WHERE id IN (...)`).

options.text: Use eager loading with a SQL JOIN or batch `IN (...)` lookup to retrieve all authors in a single query.
options.explanation: Eager loading reduces 51 queries down to 1 or 2 consolidated queries.

options.text: Increase database connection pool size to 500 connections.
options.explanation: Pool resizing does not fix inefficient O(N) query loops.

options.text: Convert all author names to uppercase in SQL.
options.explanation: String formatting does not improve I/O latency.

options.text: Add a database trigger to execute a sleep delay.
options.explanation: Delays will further degrade response latency.

questions.title: Scenario: CORS Preflight Request Failure
questions.prompt:
A frontend app hosted on `https://app.careerjourney.com` makes a `fetch()` with custom header `Authorization: Bearer <token>` to backend `https://api.careerjourney.com`. The browser console reports:
`Access to fetch has been blocked by CORS policy: Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present.`

Why did the browser trigger a preflight request and what must the backend server respond with?
questions.explanation: Requests with non-simple headers (like Authorization or application/json) trigger an automatic HTTP OPTIONS preflight request. The backend server must intercept `OPTIONS` requests and return `204/200` with headers `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.careerjourney.com` and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Authorization, Content-Type`.

options.text: The custom `Authorization` header triggers an HTTP OPTIONS preflight; the backend must respond with 200/204 and valid `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` & `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` headers.
options.explanation: Non-simple HTTP requests require successful OPTIONS preflight response with permission headers.

options.text: The user has JavaScript disabled in their browser settings.
options.explanation: CORS errors occur during browser network stack execution.

options.text: The frontend must switch from HTTPS to plain unencrypted HTTP.
options.explanation: Downgrading to HTTP compromises security and does not resolve origin domain mismatches.

options.text: CORS only applies to GET requests with URL query parameters.
options.explanation: CORS governs cross-origin requests across all HTTP verbs.

questions.title: Scenario: E-Commerce Inventory Concurrency Race Condition
questions.prompt:
During a flash sale with 1 item left in stock, two users click 'Buy Now' at the exact same millisecond. Both requests execute:
```sql
-- Step 1: Check stock
SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = 101; -- returns 1 for both
-- Step 2: Update stock
UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 101; -- both update to 0
```
Both users receive order confirmations, resulting in overselling (-1 stock). Which database mechanism guarantees atomic updates and prevents this race condition?
questions.explanation: Executing a single atomic conditional update (`UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 101 AND stock > 0`) or utilizing pessimistic locking (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) inside a transaction ensures only one transaction acquires the lock and updates successfully.

options.text: Use an atomic conditional query (`WHERE stock > 0`) or pessimistic locking with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` inside a transaction.
options.explanation: Row-level locks or atomic conditional updates guarantee stock cannot decrement past zero.

options.text: Add a 5-second `setTimeout()` delay between the SELECT and UPDATE queries.
options.explanation: Sleep timers widen the race condition window rather than fixing it.

options.text: Store inventory numbers as floating-point decimals.
options.explanation: Data types do not prevent race conditions.

options.text: Disable all database indexes on the products table.
options.explanation: Removing indexes degrades search performance and does not provide atomicity.

questions.title: Scenario: React State Batching & Stale Closures
questions.explanation: In React, state updates are batched. Because `count` is captured from the current render's closure (e.g. 0), all three calls evaluate `setCount(0 + 1)`. The correct fix is to use functional state updates: `setCount(prev => prev + 1)`.

options.text: Each call reads the same stale `count` closure value. Fix: Use functional updater form `setCount(prev => prev + 1)`.
options.explanation: Functional updates guarantee access to the most pending updated state.

questions.title: Scenario: Python Mutable Default Argument Bug
questions.prompt:
Consider the following Python function definition:
```python
def append_submission(user_id, scores=[]):
    scores.append(user_id)
    return scores

print(append_submission(101)) # Output: [101]
print(append_submission(202)) # Output: [101, 202] (Unexpected!)
```
Why is the list retained between separate function invocations?
questions.explanation: In Python, default parameter expressions are evaluated once when the function is defined, NOT each time the function is called. If a mutable object (like a list or dict) is used as a default, all calls without an explicit argument share the exact same list instance in memory. Standard fix: `scores=None` and initialize `if scores is None: scores = []`.

options.text: Default arguments are evaluated once at function definition time; the mutable list is shared across calls. Fix: Use `scores=None` and initialize inside the function body.
options.explanation: Mutable default arguments are a classic Python gotcha caused by definition-time evaluation.

options.text: Python integers are automatically cast to string arrays.
options.explanation: Python is strongly typed and does not perform implicit list conversions.

options.text: The print function alters global variables in memory.
options.explanation: print() only writes to standard output stream.

options.text: Functions in Python cannot accept more than one parameter.
options.explanation: Python functions support multiple positional and keyword arguments.

questions.title: Scenario: Git Detached HEAD State
questions.prompt:
A developer runs `git checkout a1b2c3d` (a specific commit hash) and makes several new commits. Later, they switch back to `main` and discover their new commits are missing from the branch log.
What state was the repository in, and how should they recover their commits?
questions.explanation: Checking out a commit hash directly places Git in a 'Detached HEAD' state (HEAD points directly to a commit rather than a branch ref). New commits are not associated with any named branch. They can be found using `git reflog` and recovered by creating a new branch from that commit: `git branch recovery-branch <commit-hash>`.

options.text: The repository was in 'Detached HEAD' state. Recovery: Locate commit hashes in `git reflog` and create a named branch (`git branch <name> <hash>`).
options.explanation: git reflog maintains a history of HEAD movements even for unreferenced commits.

options.text: The Git repository was corrupted and must be re-cloned from scratch.
options.explanation: Commits remain in the local object database until pruned by garbage collection.

options.text: Git commits are permanently deleted immediately after branch switching.
options.explanation: Git is append-only by default; reflog preserves orphaned commits.

options.text: Commits cannot be made without an active internet connection.
options.explanation: Git is a distributed version control system that operates offline.

questions.title: Scenario: CI/CD Pipeline Docker Permission Denied
questions.prompt:
In a GitHub Actions / GitLab CI runner script, the step `docker build -t my-app .` fails with:
`Got permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket at unix:///var/run/docker.sock`.

What is the standard Linux security cause and resolution?
questions.explanation: The user account executing the CI agent does not belong to the `docker` group (or lack read/write permissions on `/var/run/docker.sock`). Resolution: Add the runner user to the docker group via `sudo usermod -aG docker $USER` and restart the agent session.

options.text: The runner user is not in the `docker` group. Resolution: Add user to docker group (`usermod -aG docker <user>`) to grant access to `/var/run/docker.sock`.
options.explanation: Docker daemon socket ownership is restricted to root and the docker group.

options.text: Docker daemon only runs on Windows 98.
options.explanation: Docker is native to Linux containerization primitives (cgroups/namespaces).

options.text: The Dockerfile must be renamed to index.html.
options.explanation: Docker build looks specifically for Dockerfile.

options.text: The runner must delete all RAM memory before executing.
options.explanation: System RAM has no correlation with Unix socket group permissions.

The fix is to use auto-waiting assertions (e.g. `await expect(page.locator('#confirmation-modal')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 5000 })`) that poll until the element renders.

options.text: Race condition due to async network delay. Fix: Use auto-waiting assertions (`await expect(locator).toBeVisible()`) that poll until the modal appears.
options.explanation: Auto-waiting eliminates arbitrary timing race conditions in modern test frameworks.

options.explanation: Hardware specs do not cause web element race conditions.

options.explanation: Properly awaited automated tests provide consistent regression protection.

questions.prompt:
